clue.text: Welsh town top to toe with flowers — great stuff!

indicators.note: the head of the town's name is carried down to its foot, so its first letter moves to the end

parts.note: Mold is a market town in north-east Wales
asters are daisy-like garden flowers

explanation.surface: A tourist enthuses about a Welsh town covered in flowers from end to end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Welsh town' invites a long name like Llandudno; the short one wanted has its head moved to its feet by 'top to toe'. 'Great stuff' is praise for the art, not an exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: Paintings by the great European artists before about 1800 are prized works, hence great stuff.

clue.text: Horse cryptically described at sea

parts.note: read the answer as an instruction: put the word shore 'off', that is awry or jumbled, and the letters make this clue word

explanation.surface: A puzzle-setter describes a horse in a roundabout way.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: OFF (wrong, scrambled) plus SHORE describes an anagram of SHORE, which is HORSE, the clue's word. 'cryptically described' tells you to read it that way.
explanation.definitionFit: Something located out on the water away from land is said to be at sea, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Country needing prime minister without extremes?

indicators.note: the prime minister's name loses its outermost letters at both ends

parts.note: Benjamin Disraeli was a 19th-century British prime minister

explanation.surface: A nation is imagined needing a leader with no radical views.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without extremes' strips the D and I from DISRAELI; 'extremes' looks political but means the first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a nation state in the Middle East, so a straightforward example of a country.

clue.text: Entury?

parts.note: take away C (said as 'see') and the word century becomes this clue's lone word

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is the word CENTURY with its C missing: a long stretch of time, with no 'see'. Read that way, the answer is the phrase that the odd word illustrates.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a jocular greeting to someone not met for ages, and the clue pictures it as a hundred years minus a C.

clue.text: One striking perfect shot, Yorkshire opener held up by scorer

indicators.note: a container signal: the reversed pieces are gripped inside the scorer

parts.note: an etcher scores lines into a metal plate

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the pieces are read from the bottom, backwards

parts.note: an ace is a perfect unreturnable serve in tennis

indicators.note: the opening letter of the county's name is taken

explanation.surface: A cricket match report: a Yorkshire opening batsman makes a perfect stroke and is caught by the scorer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns the shot and opener together, and 'held' puts them inside; 'by' is a link. The cricket picture misleads: the scorer is an engraver, not the scorekeeper.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that grabs attention by looking striking is commonly called this, so 'one striking' describes it.

clue.text: Select film regularly repeated featuring Bob Hope

parts.note: to opt is to select or choose

indicators.note: the doubled pair has the coin set in among it, as a film features a star
the pair of letters picked from film is written out twice
every other letter of film is taken, the second and fourth

parts.note: a bob was an old British shilling, abbreviated s

explanation.surface: A cinema chooses a picture showing over and over that stars the comedian Bob Hope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes IM from fIlM, 'repeated' doubles it to IMIM, and 'featuring' slips S inside to give IMISM. Bob Hope is not the comedian: a bob was a shilling, before 1971 British money.
explanation.definitionFit: Hope and optimism both mean a confident expectation that things will turn out well.

clue.text: Did he serve wine from Churchill's cabinet?

definitions.meaning: a head manservant who looks after the wine cellar and serves at table
A senior Conservative minister in Churchill's government

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cabinet' could be a drinks cabinet in the first picture; it is the government cabinet, and R. A. Butler sat in Churchill's.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is a household servant in charge of wine; the other is the surname of a Churchill-era minister.

clue.text: May I draw your attention to a bit of skirt

parts.note: the hem is the turned-up edge of a skirt

explanation.surface: Someone politely interrupts to point out a glimpse of skirt.
explanation.definitionFit: This little throat-clearing noise is used to attract notice, exactly what the polite question asks.

clue.text: Parrot sealing fate is without a chance — all that happens to it?

indicators.note: the parrot's letters close around the rest, enclosing it

parts.note: a lory is a small brightly coloured parrot

indicators.note: the remaining letters are left to chance, so rearranged
the letter a is dropped from the words fate is

explanation.surface: A parrot's fate seems sealed with no hope of escape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' drops the A, 'chance' shuffles what is left, and 'sealing' puts it inside the parrot just after its first letter. The definition reads the answer as the whole tale of the parrot.
explanation.definitionFit: A biography of a creature recounts its whole existence, everything that happens to it from start to finish.

clue.text: Soft and luxurious

definitions.meaning: a fabric with a long soft nap, so soft to the touch

explanation.definitionFit: The word describes both velvety softness of cloth and lavish comfort, giving two separate senses.

clue.text: Wild thing 'as to go to the gallows

parts.note: a dropped-h spelling of has to, meaning must
to hang, with its h dropped in the same cockney style as the clue's ’as

explanation.surface: A dialect speaker says some wild creature has got to be hanged.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in ''as' signals a cockney accent with the h dropped, so 'go to the gallows' gives 'ANG, not HANG.
explanation.definitionFit: A mustang is a free-roaming horse of the American West, so a wild creature.

clue.text: Friend to pocket green, this for the pot

indicators.note: the friend's letters enclose the sickly word, as a pocket holds something

parts.note: chum is informal for a friend
green can mean sickly or nauseous, hence ill

explanation.surface: A friend is told to slip something green into his pocket, presumably for the pot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'green' suggests money or a snooker colour; here it means looking sick.
explanation.definitionFit: A chillum is a straight clay pipe for smoking cannabis, and pot is slang for cannabis.

clue.text: "The Sound of Music" is capital

indicators.note: the clue asks for how a word is pronounced rather than spelt

parts.note: soul is a genre of popular music

explanation.surface: Someone declares the famous musical film to be excellent.
explanation.walkthrough: The film title hides the homophone signal: the sound of SOUL music. 'is' links, and 'capital' is the city, not 'great'.
explanation.definitionFit: Seoul is the capital city of South Korea.

clue.text: Top bloke will dry up holding dry run shortly

indicators.note: the drying word wraps around the shortened rehearsal

parts.note: to parch is to dry out thoroughly

indicators.note: the rehearsal word is cut short, losing its final letter

parts.note: a trial is a rehearsal or dry run

explanation.surface: The chief warns that he'll get parched during a rehearsal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shortly' trims the rehearsal by one letter and 'holding' sets it inside the drying word after its second letter. 'Top bloke' is the chief man, not a good sort.
explanation.definitionFit: A patriarch is the male head of a family or tribe, hence the chief man or top bloke.

clue.text: Old pro offering definition for 19?

parts.note: read 19's answer, a lawyer, as one who solicits; a streetwalker fits that playful sense, and pro is slang for her

explanation.walkthrough: 19-across is SOLICITOR; split as one who solicits it describes a sex worker, and 'pro' is a short form of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A sex worker solicits clients, so she could jokingly be defined as a solicitor, and 'pro' abbreviates the word.

clue.text: Huge salamander brings misery to drinking session

parts.note: hell is a state of great misery
a bender is a drinking spree

explanation.surface: A giant amphibian goes on a binge and suffers for it.
explanation.definitionFit: The hellbender is a very large aquatic salamander of the eastern United States.

clue.text: Employing cells with cell, hot ice cream melts

indicators.note: the dessert melting loses its shape, so its letters with cell are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something about a cell next to a hot ice cream that is melting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'melts' jumbles CELL plus HOTICECREAM, fifteen letters; 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Electrochemical processes use electric cells such as batteries, so they employ cells.

clue.text: I bitch when sent up, then go silent

indicators.note: in a down entry the pieces are read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: a cat is slang for a spiteful, catty woman
a turn is a go, as in my turn

explanation.surface: Someone is mocked for being catty and then goes quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when sent up' turns I + CAT into TACI; 'sent up' looks like mockery. 'then' links.
explanation.definitionFit: A taciturn person says little, so habitually silent or uncommunicative.

clue.text: Jewish mystic troupe touring island

indicators.note: the troupe goes around the island, enclosing it

parts.note: the cast of a play is its company of actors, a troupe
Bali is an Indonesian island

explanation.surface: A Jewish mystic travels with a theatre company round an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'troupe touring' suggests travelling performers, and that is the cast, wrapped by 'touring' round the island.
explanation.definitionFit: A cabalist studies the Kabbalah, the mystical tradition of Jewish thought.

clue.text: Document writer from The Sun in charge, riot breaking out

parts.note: Sol is the Latin name for the sun

indicators.note: the riot breaks out of order, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tabloid journalist writes about a riot erupting in charge of The Sun newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun looks like the British tabloid newspaper; it is the star, SOL. 'breaking out' rearranges RIOT to ITOR; 'from' links.
explanation.definitionFit: A solicitor drafts wills, contracts and conveyancing papers, so is a writer of legal documents.

clue.text: For your answer look for "hate", perhaps

definitions.text: For your answer look for "hate", perhaps

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or behold

indicators.note: perhaps hints the word hate is to be taken loosely, its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A setter advises the solver to try the word hate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' shuffles the quoted word; the whole clue also says the answer means much the same as it, so the quoted word works twice as an &lit.
explanation.definitionFit: To loathe is to detest intensely, a near synonym of hating.

clue.text: Important man to snatch award briefly

parts.note: to nab is to grab or snatch

indicators.note: the honour is cut short, losing its final letter

parts.note: the OBE is a British honour, Officer of the Order of the British Empire

explanation.surface: A bigwig tries to grab an honour quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'briefly' cuts OBE to OB; 'to' links.
explanation.definitionFit: A nabob is a person of great wealth or importance, originally a returning Anglo-Indian grandee.

clue.text: Prayers said for some chicken — oven awaits

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Prayers are offered for a chicken bound for the oven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' links the definition to 'some'.
explanation.definitionFit: A novena is a Catholic devotion of prayers said over nine days.

clue.text: Flier achieves half height in bed

indicators.note: the shortened height goes inside the bed

parts.note: a cot is a small bed

indicators.note: only the first half of the word for height is used

parts.note: altitude means height

explanation.surface: A pilot manages half the altitude while lying in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half' takes the first four letters of the eight-letter word for height; 'in' sets them inside the bed and 'achieves' links. A coal tit is a small bird, the flier.
explanation.definitionFit: A coal tit is a small woodland bird, so a flier.

clue.text: Group providing hit

definitions.meaning: a society or association of members
to strike with a heavy stick

explanation.definitionFit: One sense is a members' society; the other is the verb meaning to strike with a cudgel.

clue.text: Vile, becoming rotten in month — throw it

indicators.note: the jumbled word goes inside the month

parts.note: Jan is short for January

indicators.note: the word vile goes bad and so changes its form, giving a rearrangement

explanation.surface: Something vile goes off during a month and should be thrown away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'becoming rotten' shuffles the four letters, set by 'in' into the abbreviated month after its second letter. 'throw it' defines by what you do with the object.
explanation.definitionFit: A javelin is a spear thrown in athletics, so the clue tells you to throw this object.

clue.text: Start to desert ship?

definitions.meaning: to start or flinch in surprise
sailors who abandon their vessel are said to ... ship

explanation.definitionFit: One sense is a sudden startled movement; the other completes the idiom for abandoning a vessel.

clue.text: Guide employer round hospital

indicators.note: the employer's letters go around the hospital abbreviation

parts.note: a user is one who employs something
H is the abbreviation for hospital on road signs

explanation.surface: A guide shows a boss round the hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'employer' looks like a boss; it means one who uses something.
explanation.definitionFit: An usher guides people to their seats in a theatre or church.
